en.title: Architecture: the whole course
en.short: What architecture is, how architecture degrees are organised, the main study areas and how to learn them well.

sections.heading: What architecture is
sections.text:
Architecture is the design of buildings and the spaces around them. It joins art, science and organisation: a building must be useful, safe, buildable, affordable and meaningful to the people who use it. Architects work with drawings, models and written specifications, and they coordinate engineers, builders, planners and clients. The subject is taught mainly through design studios, where you learn by making proposals and discussing them. It also draws on history, structures, materials, environmental science and law.

These summaries teach principles and studio habits. They do not replace a design code, a building regulation or a registered architect. Registration and building approval differ by country. In Nigeria, the Architects Registration Council of Nigeria (ARCON) regulates the profession and the Nigerian Institute of Architects (NIA) is the professional body. In the UK, the Architects Registration Board (ARB) is the statutory regulator and the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) is the professional body. Check the current law where you plan to practise.

sections.heading: How a degree is organised
sections.text:
Lengths and awards vary by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria, many universities teach a BSc in Architecture followed by a professional master’s degree; some older programmes run a longer BArch. Polytechnics offer ND and HND programmes in architectural technology, which are technician awards rather than full professional registration. In the UK, the usual route is a first degree, then a master’s, then a final professional examination, known as Parts 1, 2 and 3. Ghana and Kenya have their own patterns.

Early years build drawing, representation, history and construction. Middle years add structures, services, theory and larger studio projects. Final years add professional practice, research and a dissertation or thesis. Most courses require practical experience before full registration.

sections.heading: The main areas, in teaching order
sections.text:
Introductory topics give the tools. Design studio foundations teach the design process. Freehand drawing and visual studies train the eye and hand. Technical drawing and orthographic projection teach accurate representation. Geometry, proportion and form cover shape and order. History from prehistory to the medieval world gives context. Building materials and construction basics explain how buildings are made. Structures for architects covers statics and equilibrium. Environmental science and climate comfort introduce sun, wind and heat. Digital representation introduces CAD and BIM.

Core topics deepen these. Three studios move from small buildings to public buildings to urban and community projects. Modern and contemporary history, theory and criticism sharpen judgement. Construction detailing and structural systems make designs buildable. Building services, building physics and site planning deal with comfort, light, sound and landscape. Urban design and planning widen the scale. Sustainable design and heritage conservation add responsibility to climate and to existing buildings. Digital design covers BIM, parametric modelling and collaboration. Professional practice, ethics and contracts, building codes and planning approval, and research and critical writing prepare you for practice and for your final project.

At master’s level, advanced theory, research methods, computational design and digital fabrication, and housing and informal urbanism extend the work.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Treat studio as the centre of the course, and keep a sketchbook every day. Draw buildings you see, not only photographs. Learn to explain a design in words: what problem it solves, what you assumed, what you rejected. Read plans carefully and build simple physical models, because models reveal mistakes that drawings hide.

Keep a file of precedents with your own notes. Learn the technical content by hand before software: set out a plan, calculate a simple load, check a U-value. Visit sites and ask builders how things are fixed. Sleep and eat properly before reviews; tired work is poor work.

en.title: Architectural Design Studio: Foundations
en.short: The studio design process from brief to proposal, with space, scale, light, models and critique.

sections.heading: Brief and iteration
sections.text: A design brief states the client, users, site, activities (the programme), budget and constraints. In studio it is a starting point, not a fixed answer. The process moves between analysis, drawing, testing and revision. Iteration means repeated versions, each answering a question: Is the entrance clear? Does the room fit its furniture? Keep earlier drawings: they record decisions and help you explain them.

sections.heading: Space, scale and light
sections.text: Spatial organisation is the arrangement of rooms and open spaces and their relationships. Circulation is how people move through the building, including entrances, corridors and stairs. Good circulation separates public and private routes and avoids dead ends. Scale means size relative to the human body and to other spaces; a room may be correct in area but feel wrong if the ceiling is too low. Light includes daylight and artificial light. Note where the sun rises and sets, and place windows for activities that need light.

sections.heading: Models and critique
sections.text: Models test what drawings hide. A quick card or foam massing model (the overall shape and bulk) shows form and shadow; a detailed model at 1:100 tests room sizes and circulation. Work from simple to detailed. A design critique, or crit, is a structured review by tutors and peers. Present the brief, your intention, the evidence in drawings and models, and the trade-offs. Listen, note questions, and answer with reasons, not excuses. Criticism of the work is not criticism of you.

sections.heading: A studio case
sections.text: Suppose Ifeoma, a first-year student in Enugu, Nigeria, designs a 120 m² community reading room. The brief asks for a librarian desk, shelving, quiet reading and a meeting corner. She tests three sketch arrangements. In the chosen one, the entrance opens to the desk, circulation runs around the shelving, and quiet reading sits away from the door. She builds a 1:100 card model. At the crit she explains why the meeting corner is near the entrance: visitors can enter without crossing the quiet zone. She revises the shading after a question about afternoon glare.

keyPoints: A brief sets the client, users, site, programme, budget and constraints, but it is a starting point for testing.
Design is iterative: each drawing or model answers a question and records a decision.
Spatial organisation arranges rooms and relationships; circulation is how people move between them.
Scale relates a space to the human body and to other spaces, and light must suit the activity.
Models from simple massing to 1:100 detail test what drawings hide.
In a critique, present intention, evidence and trade-offs, and answer questions with reasons.

en.title: Freehand Drawing and Visual Studies
en.short: Observation drawing, sketching, perspective, composition and colour for recording buildings.

sections.heading: Observation and sketching
sections.text:
Observation drawing means drawing what is there, not what you assume. Compare lengths and angles with a pencil held at arm’s length, check verticals and horizontals, and study negative space, the empty shapes around and between objects. A contour line follows an edge slowly. Sketching is quick: thumbnail sketches test a view before a larger sheet. Keep a dated sketchbook, because it shows progress and feeds your portfolio.

Case: a student records a campus gate with three thumbnails, a ten-minute line sketch, then notes on materials and light. This builds visual literacy, the ability to read a place and show what matters.

sections.heading: Perspective
sections.text:
Perspective makes parallel lines appear to meet. In one-point perspective, one face of a box is parallel to the picture plane, the flat surface you draw on, and depth lines meet at one vanishing point on the horizon line, at eye level. In two-point perspective, two sets of horizontal lines meet at two vanishing points.

Keep the horizon consistent and draw construction lines lightly. Perspective helps analyse how a building meets the ground and how parts recede. It differs from orthographic projection, a separate measured system of plans and elevations.

sections.heading: Composition and colour
sections.text:
Composition is how you arrange a drawing on the page. Choose a clear subject and leave space around the building. Use foreground, middle ground and background for depth. The rule of thirds is a common guide: divide the page into three parts each way and place key elements near the lines. Vary line weight: heavier near, lighter far.

Colour records atmosphere, materials and light. Hue is the colour name, value is how light or dark it is, and saturation is how strong or grey it is. Warm colours such as red and yellow tend to advance; cool colours such as blue and green tend to recede. Use a limited palette: two or three colours plus grey. Label notes on site, such as warm ochre wall and cool grey shadow. Present portfolio sheets with title, date, place and a short analysis note.

keyPoints: Observation drawing records what is seen; check proportions, verticals, horizontals and negative space.
Thumbnail sketches and dated sketchbooks build visual literacy and portfolio evidence.
One-point perspective uses one vanishing point on the horizon; two-point uses two.
The horizon line is at eye level and must stay consistent in a drawing.
Composition arranges the page; the rule of thirds is a guide, not a law.
Hue, value and saturation describe colour; use a limited palette and label site notes.

en.title: Technical Drawing and Orthographic Projection
en.short: Orthographic views, plans, sections, elevations, scales, dimensioning and drawing conventions.

sections.heading: Projection basics
sections.text:
Orthographic projection draws an object using parallel lines of sight at right angles to a drawing plane. Each view shows true shape and size for faces parallel to that plane. A plan is the view from above. An elevation is a vertical view from front, side or rear. A section is an imaginary cut, with the cut line marked and the cut surface hatched, so hidden construction becomes visible.

First-angle and third-angle projection place the views differently. Practice varies by country, so check the title block or projection symbol.

sections.heading: Scale and dimensions
sections.text:
A scale is a ratio of drawing length to real length. At 1:50, one unit on paper represents 50 of the same unit in the building.

Example: a room 4.8 m by 3.6 m. Convert to millimetres: 4800 mm and 3600 mm. At 1:50 the drawing measures 4800 ÷ 50 = 96 mm by 3600 ÷ 50 = 72 mm. At 1:100 it measures 48 mm by 36 mm. Dimensioning gives sizes and positions with extension lines, dimension lines, arrowheads or ticks, and clear numerals. State units once, usually millimetres, and avoid repeating dimensions.

sections.heading: Drawing conventions
sections.text:
Line conventions separate what is cut, visible and hidden. Heavy continuous lines outline cut or main elements; lighter lines show visible edges; dashed lines show hidden work; centre lines mark axes and circles. Hatching shows cut materials, and different patterns may distinguish materials, but the legend must be checked.

Keep lettering legible, use a title block, north point and scale bar, and label every drawing. A scale bar remains correct after photocopying; a written ratio may not.

sections.heading: Reading a set
sections.text:
Read a drawing set in order: site plan, floor plans, elevations, sections, then details. Match grids and levels between views. Check door swings, wall thickness, stair direction and room names.

A section should agree with the plan cut line. If two views disagree, stop and ask; do not guess. Accurate reading prevents costly site errors.

keyPoints: Orthographic projection uses parallel lines of sight to give true shape and size on planes parallel to object faces.
A plan is a view from above, an elevation is a vertical view, and a section is a cut showing hidden construction.
First-angle and third-angle projection place views differently; confirm the convention from the title block.
Drawing length = real length ÷ scale denominator; a 4.8 m wall at 1:50 is 96 mm.
Use extension lines, dimension lines and clear numerals; state units once and avoid duplicate dimensions.
Line weights and hatching follow conventions, and a scale bar survives copying better than a written ratio.

en.title: Geometry, Proportion and Form
en.short: Euclidean construction, transformations, modular grids and historical proportion systems.

sections.heading: Euclidean construction
sections.text: Euclidean construction uses only a straightedge and compass. From a line and a point you can draw a perpendicular, bisect a line or angle, and build an equilateral triangle. These operations show why geometric relationships hold, not just how to draw them. In design they support accurate setting out of plans, grids and repeated shapes. A construction is exact when each step follows from a defined operation; a CAD drawing may look right but still need checking.

sections.heading: Transformations and symmetry
sections.text: A geometric transformation moves or changes a figure by a rule. Translation slides it, rotation turns it, reflection mirrors it, and scaling enlarges or reduces it. Translation, rotation and reflection preserve lengths and angles; scaling preserves angles but changes lengths by a fixed factor. Symmetry is a transformation that leaves a figure looking unchanged. These ideas help architects test facade patterns, plan layouts and repeated structural bays.

sections.heading: Modular coordination
sections.text: Modular coordination fits building dimensions to a basic module, so components and grids combine without waste. Many metric systems use a 100 mm module, but national standards differ, so check the current local standard. Example: a room 3,600 mm by 4,800 mm on a 300 mm planning module is 12 modules by 16 modules (3,600 ÷ 300 = 12; 4,800 ÷ 300 = 16). The module is a design discipline, not a rule that every building must follow.

sections.heading: Proportion systems
sections.text: Systems of proportion are sets of ratios used to relate parts to a whole. The golden section divides a line so that whole ÷ longer = longer ÷ shorter = φ ≈ 1.618, where φ = (1 + √5) ÷ 2. For a 10 m line, the longer part is 10 ÷ 1.618 = 6.18 m and the shorter is 3.82 m. Classical orders and Renaissance harmonic ratios are historical conventions, not universal rules. Use them as design tools, and judge them against function, structure and context.

keyPoints: Euclidean construction uses only a straightedge and compass to build exact figures.
Translation, rotation and reflection preserve lengths and angles; scaling changes lengths by a fixed factor.
Modular coordination counts dimensions in modules: number of modules = dimension ÷ module.
The golden section satisfies whole ÷ longer = longer ÷ shorter = φ ≈ 1.618, with φ = (1 + √5) ÷ 2.
Classical orders and the golden section are historical conventions, not universal design laws.
Check the national standard for the basic module; many metric systems use 100 mm but this varies.

en.title: History of Architecture: Prehistory to the Medieval World
en.short: How early societies used local materials, climate, belief and settlement form from prehistory to medieval times.

sections.heading: Reading early buildings
sections.text: Architecture begins with shelter, gathering and belief. Prehistoric people used caves, skin tents, timber and simple huts. When farming began in the Neolithic period, permanent villages appeared. Builders used local materials: mudbrick, sun-dried clay blocks, in dry valleys; timber in forests; stone where quarried. Climate shaped form, with thick walls and small openings in hot dry places and steep roofs in wet regions. Settlement form followed water, defence and trade. Megaliths, meaning large stones, such as tombs and Stonehenge in Britain, show careful orientation and collective effort.

sections.heading: Africa: Egypt and Aksum
sections.text: Ancient Egypt depended on the Nile. Houses and palaces were mostly mudbrick, while tombs and temples used stone to last. The pyramids at Giza, built in the Old Kingdom, express royal power and belief in an afterlife. Aksum, in modern Ethiopia and Eritrea, flourished from roughly the first to the seventh century CE. Its tall granite stelae, upright carved monuments, were cut from single blocks, and its churches show early Christian belief. Both show local stone and belief shaping monuments.

sections.heading: Great Zimbabwe
sections.text: Great Zimbabwe, in Zimbabwe, was the capital of a Shona kingdom and flourished roughly from the eleventh to the fifteenth century. Its walls are dry stone: shaped granite blocks laid without mortar. Curved walls, the Hill Complex and the Great Enclosure show planning and craft. The site used local granite and controlled trade and cattle. It is an African example of monumental architecture built from local material rather than imported stone.

sections.heading: Medieval traditions
sections.text: In Europe, the medieval period is placed between roughly the fifth and fifteenth centuries, but dates differ by region. Byzantine churches developed the dome on pendentives, curved triangular supports carrying a round dome over a square space. Romanesque buildings used thick walls and round arches. Gothic buildings used pointed arches, rib vaults and flying buttresses, external supports, to raise walls and admit light. Islamic architecture often used courtyards, columned halls and geometric ornament. Belief, climate and available materials shaped each building.

keyPoints: Early architecture responds to climate, local materials, belief and settlement needs.
Neolithic farming encouraged permanent villages and the use of mudbrick, timber and stone.
Ancient Egyptian tombs and temples used stone for permanence and belief, while ordinary buildings used mudbrick.
Aksum is known for tall granite stelae, and Great Zimbabwe for mortarless dry-stone walls.
Byzantine, Romanesque, Gothic and Islamic buildings each used structure and ornament to serve worship and climate.
Period names and dates differ by region, so avoid treating European medieval styles as universal.

en.title: Building Materials and Construction Basics
en.short: Masonry, concrete, timber, steel and glass, plus simple foundations, walls, floors and roofs.

sections.heading: Materials and properties
sections.text: Masonry means brick, block or stone laid with mortar. It is strong in compression, durable and good for walls, but weak in tension. Concrete is a mix of cement, sand, coarse aggregate and water. It is strong in compression and weak in tension, so reinforced concrete adds steel bars. Timber is strong along the grain and light, but it moves with moisture and needs protection from fire, rot and insects. Steel is strong in both tension and compression and can span far, but it needs corrosion and fire protection. Glass is transparent and brittle; it lets in light but must be used as safe glazing where people can touch it. No material is best in every way.

sections.heading: Simple elements
sections.text: Foundations transfer building loads to the ground. Shallow strip and pad footings suit firm soil; deep piles reach stronger layers. Walls enclose or divide space and may carry loads. Floors are ground-bearing slabs or suspended slabs on beams. Roofs shed rain and sun; a slope helps drainage, and trusses or beams support the covering. These elements work as a system: a heavy roof needs stronger walls and foundations, while a light steel frame may allow wider openings and faster assembly.

sections.heading: Choice shapes design
sections.text: Material choice shapes span, opening size, speed, maintenance and comfort. A made-up case: architect Amina designs a two-storey clinic in Kano with cement block walls, a reinforced concrete frame, timber roof trusses and glass windows. The frame carries loads, blocks enclose rooms, timber is light and workable, and glass gives daylight. On a humid coastal site, she would detail more protection for timber and steel. Codes and standards differ by country; check the current local building code and approval rules.

keyPoints: Masonry is strong in compression and suits walls, but it is weak in tension.
Concrete is strong in compression and needs steel reinforcement to resist tension.
Timber is strong along the grain but needs protection from moisture, fire and insects.
Steel is strong and ductile but needs fire and corrosion protection; glass is brittle and must be used safely.
Foundations transfer loads to the ground, while walls, floors and roofs enclose, span and shelter.
Material choice depends on span, climate, cost, skills, maintenance and local availability, and codes differ by country.

en.title: Structures for Architects: Statics and Equilibrium
en.short: Forces, moments, equilibrium, loads and simple beam and truss behaviour for architects.

sections.heading: Forces and equilibrium
sections.text: A force is a push or pull measured in newtons (N). It has size and direction, so it is a vector. Statics studies bodies at rest. Equilibrium means the resultant force and moment are zero. In two dimensions: ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0 and ΣM = 0. A free-body diagram shows all external forces and reactions. A roller gives one reaction, a pin gives two, and a fixed support also gives a moment.

sections.heading: Moments and reactions
sections.text: A moment is the turning effect of a force: M = F × d, where d is the perpendicular distance from the pivot. Units are newton metres (N·m). Example: a 6 m beam carries a 12 kN point load 2 m from the left support. Take moments about the left support: R_B × 6 = 12 × 2, so R_B = 4 kN. Vertical equilibrium gives R_A = 12 − 4 = 8 kN. Check: 8 + 4 = 12. The bending moment under the load is 8 × 2 = 16 kN·m.

sections.heading: Loads and beams
sections.text: Loads are dead (permanent self-weight), live (people and furniture) and environmental (wind, snow, earthquake). Codes define them and differ by country, so check the local code. Loads travel from slab to beam to column to foundation. A beam bends: one face is in compression, the other in tension. Shear force and bending moment diagrams show internal actions. For a simply supported beam, central point load P gives PL ÷ 4; uniform load w gives wL² ÷ 8.

sections.heading: Trusses and form
sections.text: A truss is a framework of straight members joined at pins, forming triangles. If loads act only at joints, members carry mainly axial force: tension (pulling) or compression (pushing). Triangulation stops the shape distorting. A top chord may be in compression while a diagonal is in tension. Structure shapes architecture: deep beams and trusses allow long spans, arches carry load mainly in compression, and columns collect vertical load. Early checks of span and load path guide form.

keyPoints: Equilibrium in two dimensions requires ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0 and ΣM = 0.
A moment is force times perpendicular distance: M = F × d.
For a simply supported beam with a central point load P over span L, the maximum bending moment is PL ÷ 4.
For a uniform load w over span L, the maximum bending moment is wL² ÷ 8.
Truss members under joint loads carry mainly axial tension or compression, and triangulation keeps the shape stable.
Loads follow a path from slab to beam to column to foundation, and load codes differ by country.

en.title: Environmental Science and Climate Comfort
en.short: Climate elements, sun paths, wind, thermal comfort and passive design for buildings.

sections.heading: Climate elements
sections.text: Weather is the day-to-day state of the atmosphere; climate is the pattern over many years. The main climate elements for design are solar radiation, air temperature, humidity, wind and precipitation. Local records from the meteorological agency give design values, which differ by place. A building also creates a microclimate: a shaded courtyard, planted screen or hot paved yard changes temperature, wind and glare. Climate zones (hot-dry, hot-humid, composite, temperate, cold) guide early decisions, but site data must be checked.

sections.heading: Sun paths
sections.text: A sun path diagram shows the sun’s apparent track for a latitude and date. Altitude is height above the horizon; azimuth is compass direction. Near the equator the midday sun is high all year and can be north or south of the zenith. Noon altitude is 90° − |latitude − declination|, where declination is the sun’s angle north or south of the equator. At latitude 10°N, it is 80° at the equinox, 76.5° at the June solstice and 56.5° at the December solstice. These angles set shading depth.

sections.heading: Thermal comfort
sections.text: Thermal comfort is the condition of mind that expresses satisfaction with the thermal environment. It depends on air temperature, mean radiant temperature (surrounding surface temperature), humidity, air speed, clothing and activity. Moving air can make a higher air temperature feel acceptable if surfaces are cool. Wind removes heat and moisture from the skin. Prevailing winds and local breezes affect ventilation. Inlets should face the prevailing breeze with an outlet opposite for cross ventilation; trees and buildings can block it.

sections.heading: Passive design
sections.text: Passive design uses form and envelope to keep comfort without mechanical systems. Hot-dry: compact form, thick walls, small shaded openings and thermal mass (heavy materials store heat) slow heat gain and reduce swings. Hot-humid: elongated form, large shaded openings and cross ventilation remove heat and moisture. Orientation, shading, insulation and light roofs reduce solar gain. A school in northern Nigeria might run east-west, shade north and south walls and open windows to the prevailing breeze.

keyPoints: Climate is long-term weather; design uses local climate data for solar radiation, temperature, humidity, wind and precipitation.
Sun path diagrams give altitude and azimuth; noon altitude = 90° − |latitude − declination|.
Thermal comfort depends on air temperature, mean radiant temperature, humidity, air speed, clothing and activity.
Passive design uses orientation, shading, thermal mass, insulation and natural ventilation before mechanical systems.
Compact forms suit hot-dry climates; elongated, cross-ventilated forms suit hot-humid climates.
Building regulations and climate data differ by country, so check the current local source.

en.title: Digital Representation: CAD and BIM Basics
en.short: 2D drafting, 3D modelling, layers, scale and the basic ideas of BIM.

sections.heading: CAD and 2D drafting
sections.text: CAD (computer-aided design) is software for drawing with precise vector geometry: lines and shapes stored as coordinates, not pixels. In two-dimensional drafting you draw plans, sections and elevations in model space, the main drawing area, usually at full size. Layers group related elements, such as walls, doors and dimensions, and each layer can carry its own colour, lineweight and visibility setting. Scale is set when the drawing is printed or placed on a sheet. At 1:100, one unit on paper represents 100 units in reality. Example: a 3,000 mm wall is drawn at 3,000 mm, then plotted at 3,000 ÷ 100 = 30 mm.

sections.heading: 3D modelling
sections.text: Three-dimensional modelling adds the vertical axis. A wall becomes a solid with length, thickness and height, and the software can generate plans and sections from it. Solids have volume; surfaces have area but no thickness. Coordinates (x, y, z) locate every point, so a window can be placed exactly. Perspective views and simple renders help you test form and shadow, but they are presentations, not construction information. Keep the model tidy: name objects, purge unused items and save versions.

sections.heading: BIM basics
sections.text: BIM (building information modelling) is a process, not just software. Objects carry information: a door knows its width, fire rating and manufacturer. Because the model is shared, a change to a wall can update plans, schedules and quantities. Clash detection finds conflicts, such as a pipe crossing a beam, before construction. IFC (Industry Foundation Classes) is an open file format for exchanging models between different software. Agree file names, folder structure and revision dates at the start. Standards and registration rules differ by country, so check the current local requirement.

keyPoints: CAD stores geometry as precise coordinates, not pixels.
Draw at full size in model space and set scale when plotting.
Layers group elements and control colour, lineweight and visibility.
3D solids have volume; surfaces have area but no thickness.
BIM objects carry information, so plans, schedules and quantities can update together.
IFC is an open format for exchanging models between software.

en.title: Architectural Design Studio: Small Buildings
en.short: From brief and site to an integrated small-building proposal: plan, section, structure, services and access.

sections.heading: Brief and site
sections.text: A small building begins with a brief: the client’s needs, budget and constraints written as rooms, areas, relationships and priorities. Site analysis records orientation, sun and wind, levels, drainage, soil, access, neighbours, trees and services. Together they define the design problem. Drawing the plan before testing the site is a common mistake. At domestic scale small moves matter: a corridor wastes area, a shaded veranda cools a house, and a step excludes a wheelchair user.

sections.heading: Integrated proposal
sections.text:
The proposal is integrated when plan, section, structure, services and access agree. Plan shows rooms and circulation; section shows heights, stairs, roof and light. Structure must suit the span: loadbearing walls for short spans, beams or frames for longer ones. Services need routes: water in, drainage out, electricity, ventilation. Accessibility means step-free entrance, level thresholds, a usable toilet and turning space; exact dimensions vary by country and code, so check the local building regulations. In Nigeria, architects register with ARCON and engineers with COREN; registration and codes differ elsewhere.

Case: a two-bedroom house for the Adeyemi family in Ibadan, Nigeria, on a 450 m² plot. The footprint is 90 m², so coverage is 90 ÷ 450 = 20%. The service core sits on the west wall to buffer afternoon heat, and the living room faces north-east for morning light.

sections.heading: Presentation
sections.text: Presentation is part of design, not decoration. A standard set includes site plan, floor plans, sections, elevations, a 3D view, a physical model and a short design statement. Drawings must be consistent: a door shown on plan must appear in section, and a beam must have a support. Tutors and clients read the set as one argument. Label materials, levels and key dimensions, and keep the drawing legible in black and white.

keyPoints: A brief turns client needs into rooms, areas and priorities.
Site analysis tests orientation, levels, drainage, access and neighbours before planning.
An integrated proposal keeps plan, section, structure, services and access consistent.
Span and layout decide whether walls, beams or frames carry the load.
Accessibility dimensions and registration rules vary by country, so check the local authority and professional body.
A presentation set is read as one argument, so drawings must agree.

en.title: Architectural Design Studio: Public Buildings
en.short: Complex public building programmes, circulation, egress, accessibility and coordinated servicing.

sections.heading: Programme and context
sections.text: A public building serves users and activities at once, so the studio begins with the programme. The programme is the schedule of spaces, their areas, adjacencies and relationships. A complex programme has many interdependent parts, such as a library with reading rooms, classrooms, a café, offices and plant. Context means the site, climate, culture, neighbours and movement around the building. User needs include ages, abilities and travel modes. Test the brief against real journeys, not just a list of rooms.

sections.heading: Circulation and egress
sections.text: Circulation is the network of movement: entrances, corridors, stairs, lifts and lobbies. Separate public, private and service routes so visitors avoid staff areas and kitchens. Make routes legible. Egress means escape in an emergency: protected routes, exits and assembly points. Accessibility means people with disabilities can enter and use the building independently, with step-free routes, clear widths, accessible toilets and lifts. These rules differ by country, so check the national building code and local authority; do not copy limits from another country.

sections.heading: Servicing and coordination
sections.text: Servicing covers the systems that keep the building working: ventilation, electrical power, water, drainage, fire detection, ICT and waste. Coordinate these with structure early. A regular grid gives predictable spans, but large public spaces may need longer spans or different floor-to-floor heights. Plant rooms, risers, ducts and ceiling voids need space. If added late, ceilings drop and rooms lose height. Coordinated drawings or a shared model help find clashes before construction.

sections.heading: Studio case
sections.text: Case: a made-up community library and skills centre in Kano, 2,400 m². The brief has a reading room, children’s room, computer lab, two classrooms, offices, café, toilets and plant. Public rooms sit near the entrance, staff and stores behind, service access at the side. Two protected escape stairs serve the upper floor, and a step-free route links entrance, lift and toilets. A 7.2 m structural grid suits classrooms and reading room; ducts run above corridors. Check egress and accessibility against Nigeria’s National Building Code and Kano planning rules.

keyPoints: Programme is the schedule of spaces, areas, adjacencies and relationships that drives a public building design.
Separate public, private and service circulation so users and staff move safely and logically.
Egress is emergency escape and accessibility is independent use; both are regulated and differ by country.
Coordinate structure and building services early so plant, ducts and risers fit without lowering ceilings.
Test the brief against context and real user journeys, not just a room list.
Check the current national building code and local planning rules before fixing egress, accessibility and servicing details.

en.title: Architectural Design Studio: Urban and Community Projects
en.short: This summary covers block and neighbourhood design: public space, density, mixed use and community participation.

sections.heading: Scale and streets
sections.text: At block or neighbourhood scale, the studio asks how buildings make a public realm: the streets, squares and open spaces between them. Urban design arranges buildings, streets and spaces so they work together. A proposal should show street edges, entrances and active frontage, meaning ground-floor uses such as shops that face and open onto the street. Permeability, the ease of walking through an area, and legibility, how easily people understand where they are, are useful tests. Drawings often include a figure-ground plan, with built form solid and open space void, and a street section showing height against width.

sections.heading: Density and mix
sections.text: Density is the amount of development on a site. It may be measured as dwellings per hectare or as plot ratio (floor area ratio), total floor area divided by site area. Definitions and acceptable levels differ by country and local plan, so check the current planning authority. Mixed use combines homes, shops, workplaces, schools or community facilities in one building or block. It can shorten trips and keep streets busy at different hours, but needs careful servicing, noise control and access. Example: a made-up scheme in Kano, Nigeria, has 120 homes on 2 hectares. That is 60 dwellings per hectare. If homes average 80 m², total floor area is 9,600 m²; plot ratio is 9,600 ÷ 20,000 = 0.48.

sections.heading: Participation and proposal
sections.text: Community participation means involving residents and users in decisions, not only informing them. Methods include meetings, walks, interviews, mapping and design workshops. It can reveal how space is used and who may be excluded. The final output is an urban design proposal: plans, sections, perspectives and a written explanation that connect buildings to streets and public life. State assumptions and check them against local planning rules. Professional registration and design codes differ by country. In Nigeria, architects register with the Architects Registration Council of Nigeria (ARCON); COREN regulates engineering. Do not assume another country’s limits apply.

keyPoints: Urban design at block scale arranges buildings, streets and public spaces so they work together.
Active frontage means ground-floor uses that face and open onto the street; permeability and legibility are useful tests.
Density can be measured as dwellings per hectare; plot ratio = total floor area ÷ site area.
Mixed use combines homes, shops, workplaces or community facilities, but needs servicing, noise control and access.
Community participation involves residents in decisions through meetings, walks, interviews, mapping and workshops.
Professional registration and design codes differ by country; in Nigeria architects register with ARCON and COREN regulates engineering.

en.title: History of Modern and Contemporary Architecture
en.short: From nineteenth-century industrial cities to modernism, postmodernism and African contemporary practice.

sections.heading: Industrial roots and modernism
sections.text: Modern architecture grew from the industrial city. New materials such as iron, steel and reinforced concrete, plus mass housing and transport, challenged historic styles. The Bauhaus (founded in Germany in 1919) joined craft to industry. The CIAM meetings, from 1928, promoted functional planning. The term International Style came from a 1932 exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art in New York. Modernism treated form as following function and society, but it also reflected politics and economies.

sections.heading: Modernism beyond Europe
sections.text: Modernism travelled through empire, trade and education. In Africa, independence-era governments used modern civic buildings, universities and housing to signal development. Architects adapted concrete frames, shading and cross-ventilation to tropical climates, often called tropical modernism. Postcolonial architecture is the built work and debate after colonial rule; it asks whose values a building serves. A case is Brasília, planned by Lúcio Costa and Oscar Niemeyer and inaugurated in 1960. Its public buildings and zoning expressed national progress, yet critics noted car dependence and distant workers’ housing.

sections.heading: Postmodern critique
sections.text: Postmodernism from the 1960s rejected modernism’s claimed universality. Robert Venturi’s Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture (1966) and Learning from Las Vegas (1972, with Denise Scott Brown and Steven Izenour) valued symbolism, ornament and ordinary commercial signs. Jane Jacobs criticised large-scale urban renewal in The Death and Life of Great American Cities (1961), defending mixed streets and local life. Postmodern buildings often quote historical forms playfully. The movement was less a single style than a critique of expert planning.

sections.heading: Contemporary practice
sections.text: Contemporary practice is plural. Architects work with global clients, digital tools, sustainability and heritage. Adaptive reuse keeps existing structures and reduces waste. Informal settlements and climate risk push designers to work with residents rather than only for them. African contemporary architecture includes both large civic projects and small community buildings. The social question remains: who commissions, who uses and who is excluded? Design codes and professional registration differ by country; for example, the Architects Registration Council of Nigeria (ARCON) registers architects in Nigeria. Check national rules.

keyPoints: Modern architecture responded to industrialisation, new materials and social reform.
CIAM and the International Style spread functional planning internationally.
Postcolonial and tropical modernism adapted modern forms to climate and nation-building in Africa.
Postmodernism criticised modernism’s universal claims and valued symbolism, context and ordinary city life.
Brasília shows both the ambition and social costs of planned modernist cities.
Contemporary practice is plural, linking sustainability, heritage, digital tools and social inclusion.

en.title: Architectural Theory and Criticism
en.short: Space, form, function, meaning, representation and experience, and how to read and write about buildings.

sections.heading: Reading architecture
sections.text: Criticism begins with careful description before judgement. A critic records what is there: site, structure, materials, light, circulation and use. Then comes analysis, which explains how parts relate. Interpretation proposes meaning. Evaluation judges success against stated aims, not personal taste alone. Keep description, interpretation and judgement separate so readers can see your evidence. Read texts the same way: identify the claim, evidence and assumptions.

sections.heading: Space and form
sections.text: Space is the void people occupy and move through; it is shaped by enclosure, threshold, scale and light. Form is the visible arrangement of mass, geometry and surface. Scale concerns size relative to the body; proportion concerns relations among dimensions. Form and space work together: a low dark entrance can make a tall hall feel larger. Function, or programme, is the pattern of activities a building supports. Good function includes fit, safety and adaptability, not only efficiency.

sections.heading: Meaning and experience
sections.text: Meaning arises from symbols, materials, building types and cultural memory, and it may differ between designer and user. Experience is bodily and sensory: approach, sound, temperature, smell and memory all shape it. Representation, through drawings, models, photographs and words, never simply copies a building; it selects and persuades. Ask what a drawing includes, omits and makes easy to imagine.

sections.heading: A critical example
sections.text: Suppose a new market hall in Kano is praised for its bold roof. A critical reading asks: Does the roof shade the stalls? Does circulation separate traders and buyers safely? What does the concrete frame say about permanence or civic pride? Do traders experience the space as theirs? Write a thesis, support it with observed evidence, acknowledge a counterargument, and cite sources properly. This structure turns opinion into an argument others can test.

keyPoints: Criticism separates description, analysis, interpretation and evaluation.
Space is shaped by enclosure, threshold, scale and light; form is the arrangement of mass, geometry and surface.
Function, or programme, is the pattern of activities supported, including safety and adaptability.
Meaning depends on symbols, materials, building types and cultural memory, and may differ between designer and user.
Representation in drawings, models and photographs selects and persuades rather than copying neutrally.
Good criticism states a thesis, gives evidence, answers a counterargument and cites sources.

en.title: Building Construction and Detailing
en.short: How walls, floors, roofs, stairs and envelopes are assembled, detailed and made weathertight.

sections.heading: Assemblies and junctions
sections.text: Construction detailing turns a design into buildable assemblies: walls, floors, roofs, stairs and windows. A detail is an enlarged drawing showing how parts meet. At a junction, such as wall to floor or roof to wall, each layer must remain continuous: structure, insulation, waterproofing, vapour control and finish. A damp-proof course (DPC) stops rising damp; a flashing sheds rainwater at an edge or penetration. Wet rooms need falls to drains, tanking (a sealed waterproof layer) or a membrane, and upstands (raised edges) at walls. Roofs need correct laps and drainage. These principles are general; product systems and code limits differ by country, so check the manufacturer and local authority.

sections.heading: Envelope control
sections.text: The building envelope separates inside from outside. Thermal control means insulating the envelope and avoiding thermal bridges, where a poor junction lets heat bypass insulation. Moisture control means keeping water out and letting vapour escape. A vapour control layer restricts vapour from entering the construction; ventilation removes moisture. Condensation risk depends on temperature, humidity and the order of layers. In hot humid climates, the strategy differs from cold climates. Waterproofing must be continuous and protected.

sections.heading: Stairs and tolerances
sections.text: Stairs are checked by rise (height of one step) and going (tread depth). A common comfort rule is 2R + G = 600 to 650 mm, but local codes set limits. Example: floor-to-floor height 3,000 mm. With riser R = 150 mm, number of risers = 3,000 ÷ 150 = 20. If going G = 300 mm, 2R + G = 600 mm. There are 19 treads between floors. Tolerances are allowed variations in position or size. They cover setting out, structure and finishes, and movement joints allow expansion.

sections.heading: Drawing details
sections.text: Details are drawn at scales such as 1:20, 1:10 or 1:5, with levels, dimensions, materials and references. They must show the sequence of construction and who builds what. Coordinated details avoid clashes between structure, services and finishes.

keyPoints: A detail is an enlarged drawing that shows how parts of an assembly meet.
At every junction, structure, insulation, waterproofing, vapour control and finish should remain continuous.
Waterproofing relies on falls, laps, upstands and protection; DPCs and flashings keep water out.
Thermal bridges and air leakage weaken the envelope, while vapour control and ventilation manage moisture.
The stair rule 2R + G = 600 to 650 mm is common, but local codes set the limits.
Tolerances and movement joints allow for building and material movement; check local standards and manufacturer details.

en.title: Structural Systems for Architects
en.short: Load paths, frames, trusses, shells, cables and foundations, and coordinating with engineers.

sections.heading: Load paths
sections.text:
A load path is the route a force takes from where it acts to the ground. Slab to beam to column to foundation is common. Loads include dead (self-weight) and live (people, furniture) types. Designers often use tributary area: the floor area that feeds one member.

Example: a 6 m × 4 m slab carries 5 kN/m² and spans one way across the 4 m width onto two beams along the 6 m edges. Total load = 6 × 4 × 5 = 120 kN. Each beam takes half: 60 kN, or 60 ÷ 6 = 10 kN/m. Each end column then receives 30 kN from that beam.

sections.heading: Frames and trusses
sections.text:
A frame has beams and columns joined to resist bending. Rigid joints keep angles fixed; pinned or braced frames rely on bracing for stability.

A truss is a triangulated frame whose members carry mainly axial force, tension or compression, so it is efficient over long spans. Architects set the grid and span; engineers size members. Deeper structures suit longer spans but reduce ceiling height.

sections.heading: Shells and cables
sections.text:
A shell is a thin curved surface that carries load mainly by membrane action, in compression, tension or both. It needs edge supports and stiffness against buckling.

A cable carries only tension and takes its shape from the load, so it needs strong anchorages and often a stiffening system. Both can enclose large spaces with little material, but their geometry must be designed early.

sections.heading: Foundations and coordination
sections.text:
Foundations transfer loads to the ground. Shallow forms include pad, strip and raft; deep forms include piles. Soil strength and settlement guide the choice, so site investigation is essential.

Architects coordinate by fixing grids, levels and structural zones, and by involving the engineer before spatial decisions harden. Codes, titles and registration differ by country; in Nigeria, for example, engineering registration is through COREN. Check local requirements.

keyPoints: A load path carries force from slab to beam to column to foundation.
Tributary area is the floor area feeding one member; total load = area × load per m².
Frames resist bending at joints; trusses use triangulation and mainly axial force.
Shells carry load by membrane action; cables carry tension only and need anchorages.
Foundations may be shallow (pad, strip, raft) or deep (piles), chosen from soil and load.
Coordinate grids, levels and structural zones with the engineer early; codes and registration vary by country.

en.title: Building Services and Environmental Systems
en.short: Water, drainage, electrical, lighting, HVAC, fire and lift services, and how to integrate them in design.

sections.heading: Water and drainage
sections.text: Potable water is drinking water. Supply needs storage tanks, pumps, pressure and pipes, often in risers. Drainage carries foul water from toilets and surface water from roofs. Sanitation fixtures need traps and ventilated soil stacks. Space is needed for tanks, plant, inspection chambers and pipe risers. Falls on drainage pipes depend on local codes; check them.

sections.heading: Electrical and lighting
sections.text:
Electrical services bring supply to a main board, then distribute to sockets, equipment, data and earthing. Loads must be balanced and protected. Artificial lighting uses luminaires; lux is illuminance, while lumens measure lamp output. The simplified lumen method estimates the number of luminaires: N = (E × A) ÷ (F × UF × MF), where E is illuminance in lux, A is area in m², F is lumens per luminaire, UF is utilisation factor and MF is maintenance factor.

Example: a 6 m × 4 m room (24 m²) at 300 lux, with 3000 lm luminaires, UF 0.6 and MF 0.8: N = (300 × 24) ÷ (3000 × 0.6 × 0.8) = 7200 ÷ 1440 = 5 luminaires. Check local standards and manufacturer data.

sections.heading: Heating, cooling, fire
sections.text: Heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) control temperature, humidity and air quality. In hot climates cooling and ventilation dominate; in cold climates heating does. Ducts, chillers, boilers and air-handling units need plant rooms and ceiling voids. Fire protection has passive measures (compartmentation, escape stairs) and active measures (detection, alarms, sprinklers, hydrants). Escape routes must be clear and protected. Codes differ by country.

sections.heading: Vertical transport and coordination
sections.text: Lifts and escalators need shafts, machine rooms or overhead space, and waiting areas. Lift numbers and sizes depend on traffic and local standards. All services must be coordinated early: risers, ducts, cable trays, pipes and shafts compete for space. Use service zones and ceiling voids, allow maintenance access, and check clashes before construction. Design codes and professional registration differ by country; in Nigeria, COREN registers engineers. Check current local requirements.

keyPoints: Building services need planned horizontal and vertical distribution space, such as risers, plant rooms and ceiling voids.
Drainage needs falls, traps and ventilation; check local code requirements.
Lighting estimate: N = (E × A) ÷ (F × UF × MF), with E in lux, A in m² and F in lumens.
HVAC plant and ductwork need space and early coordination with structure and ceilings.
Fire protection combines passive compartmentation and escape with active detection and suppression.
Lifts and escalators need shafts, machine space and traffic planning; coordinate all services before construction.

en.title: Building Physics: Thermal, Light and Acoustic Environments
en.short: Heat, thermal comfort, daylight, lighting and sound control in buildings.

sections.heading: Heat and comfort
sections.text: Heat moves by conduction, convection and radiation. For a wall, q = U × A × ΔT, where U is thermal transmittance (W/m²K), A area and ΔT temperature difference. U = 1 ÷ ΣR (total resistance, including surface resistances), and each layer has resistance R = d ÷ k. Example: a 10 m² wall with U = 0.5 W/m²K and ΔT = 10 K loses q = 0.5 × 10 × 10 = 50 W. Thermal comfort depends on air and radiant temperature, humidity, air speed, clothing and activity. Fanger’s PMV/PPD (predicted mean vote and predicted percentage dissatisfied) predicts comfort in conditioned rooms; adaptive comfort applies to naturally ventilated buildings. Limits differ by standard and country.

sections.heading: Daylight and lighting
sections.text: Daylight factor (DF) = indoor illuminance ÷ outdoor horizontal illuminance × 100 under an overcast sky. It shows how much daylight reaches a point; recommended values vary by room use and climate. Artificial lighting uses luminous flux (lumens), illuminance (lux) and efficacy (lumens per watt). The lumen method gives N = E × A ÷ (F × UF × MF), where E is target illuminance, A floor area, F flux per luminaire, UF utilisation factor and MF maintenance factor. Example: a 20 m² room, E = 300 lx, F = 3000 lm, UF = 0.6, MF = 0.8 gives N = 300 × 20 ÷ (3000 × 0.6 × 0.8) = 4.17, so use 5 luminaires. Check local standards for target levels.

sections.heading: Sound and design
sections.text: Sound is pressure variation, measured in decibels: L = 20 log₁₀(p ÷ p₀), with p₀ = 20 µPa. Noise control works at source, along the path and at the receiver. Insulation reduces transmission; absorption reduces reflection. Reverberation time T = 0.161 V ÷ A (metric), where V is room volume and A is total absorption in m² sabins. Design choices include orientation and shading, insulation and ventilation, window size and glare control, efficient lamps, and separating noisy rooms from quiet ones. Codes and comfort standards differ by country, so check the official source.

keyPoints: Heat loss through a wall is q = U × A × ΔT, with U = 1 ÷ ΣR (including surface resistances) and R = d ÷ k.
Thermal comfort depends on air and radiant temperature, humidity, air speed, clothing and activity; comfort standards differ by country.
Daylight factor = indoor illuminance ÷ outdoor horizontal illuminance × 100.
Lumen method: N = E × A ÷ (F × UF × MF).
Sound level L = 20 log₁₀(p ÷ p₀), with p₀ = 20 µPa; control noise at source, path and receiver.
Reverberation time T = 0.161 V ÷ A (metric), where A is total absorption in m² sabins.

en.title: Site Planning and Landscape Design
en.short: Site analysis, access, grading, drainage, earthworks, vegetation and outdoor space design.

sections.heading: Site analysis
sections.text: Site analysis is the study of a plot before design: boundaries, contours (lines of equal level), slope, soil, drainage, sun path, prevailing wind, climate, views, noise, access, services and neighbouring uses. A site plan records these. Building placement should follow the evidence. In a hot climate, shade and breeze may matter; on a slope, the building may step with the land. Planning rules on setbacks, coverage and access differ by country, so check the local planning authority.

sections.heading: Access and earthworks
sections.text: Access means how people, vehicles and services reach the site, including the entrance, turning space and pedestrian route. Grading is shaping the ground to levels. Earthworks are the cut and fill needed to make those levels. Cut removes soil; fill adds it. Balance cut and fill where possible, strip and store topsoil, and compact fill in layers. Example: a 20 m × 15 m platform on a uniform 5% slope falls 20 × 0.05 = 1.0 m along its length. Set at mean ground level, average cut and fill depth is 0.25 m over each half. Volume = 10 × 15 × 0.25 = 37.5 m³ cut and 37.5 m³ fill. On difficult ground, get geotechnical advice.

sections.heading: Drainage and landscape
sections.text: Drainage moves rainwater safely away from buildings and paths. Use ground slopes, gutters, swales (shallow grass channels), soakaways (pits that let water soak into the ground) and permeable paving where suitable, and check local rules. Vegetation can shade, cool, screen and stabilise soil. Keep mature trees and native species, and protect roots during work. Outdoor space design arranges paths, seating, planting and boundaries so spaces are usable, safe and easy to maintain. Local climate and maintenance needs should guide planting. Landscape is part of the building design, not a final decoration.

keyPoints: Site analysis records boundaries, contours, slope, soil, drainage, climate, access and neighbours before design.
Building placement should respond to slope, sun, wind, views, noise and local planning rules; rules differ by country.
Grading shapes levels; earthworks are cut and fill, and balancing them reduces carting.
For a rectangular platform on uniform slope, fall = length × slope; cut or fill volume ≈ area × average depth.
Drainage should move rainwater away from buildings using slopes, swales, soakaways or permeable paving, subject to local rules.
Vegetation and outdoor space design should be planned with the building, not added at the end.

en.title: Urban Design and Planning
en.short: Urban form, land use, density, transport, public space and planning frameworks.

sections.heading: City form and morphology
sections.text: Urban morphology is the study of a city’s physical pattern: streets, blocks, plots and building types, and how they change over time. A grid, a radial road system or an organic lane network each shapes movement and land value. Architecture matters because each building meets the street, casts shadow and adds or reduces activity. A row of shops with doors on the pavement supports street life; a blank wall does not. Morphology helps you read why a place feels the way it does before you propose change.

sections.heading: Density and land use
sections.text:
Land use is what happens on land: housing, shops, offices, industry, parks or mixed use. Zoning sets allowed uses, often in a plan. Density measures how many people or dwellings occupy an area. Floor area ratio (FAR), also called plot ratio, measures building intensity: FAR = total floor area ÷ site area. Coverage = building footprint ÷ site area.

Example: a 0.5 ha site (5,000 m²) has a 1,000 m² footprint and four floors, so floor area = 4,000 m². FAR = 4,000 ÷ 5,000 = 0.8. Coverage = 1,000 ÷ 5,000 = 0.20, or 20%. With 50 dwellings, density = 50 ÷ 0.5 = 100 dwellings per hectare.

sections.heading: Transport, public space and planning
sections.text: Transport networks connect land uses. A street hierarchy separates quiet local streets from busy main roads; public transport, walking and cycling need safe routes and good connections to buildings. Public space includes streets, squares, parks and markets. Good public space is accessible, overlooked and comfortable; Jane Jacobs argued that streets watched by people in nearby buildings are safer and livelier ('eyes on the street'). Planning frameworks guide growth through plans, zoning, development control (checking that proposed building work follows the rules) and public participation. The law differs by country: in the UK, a local planning authority grants planning permission; in Nigeria, state and local planning authorities administer development control. Professional registration differs too: in Nigeria, ARCON registers architects and COREN registers engineers. Always check the current national and local rules.

keyPoints: Urban morphology links street, plot and building patterns to city form.
Density = dwellings ÷ area; FAR = total floor area ÷ site area; coverage = footprint ÷ site area.
Zoning and land-use plans decide which uses are allowed and where.
Transport, public space and building entrances shape how a place is used.
Planning frameworks include plans, zoning, development control and public participation.
Planning law and professional registration differ by country; check current official rules.

en.title: Sustainable Design and Climate-Responsive Architecture
en.short: Passive design, energy and water efficiency, materials, life-cycle thinking, adaptation and green rating systems.

sections.heading: Passive design
sections.text: Sustainable design reduces environmental harm and improves comfort over a building’s life. Passive design uses form, orientation, envelope and landscape to manage sun, air and heat without relying on mechanical systems. Thermal mass is the ability of a material to store heat. In hot-humid climates, shade, cross-ventilation and light roofs help; in hot-dry climates, thermal mass, small openings and night cooling help; in temperate and cold climates, insulation, solar gain and airtightness matter. For example, a two-storey clinic in Kano, Nigeria, could run its long axis east-west, add deep verandahs and high-level vents to shade walls and release hot air.

sections.heading: Efficiency and materials
sections.text: Energy efficiency means delivering the same service with less energy: reduce demand first, then use efficient equipment, then add renewable supply. Water efficiency includes low-flow fittings, rainwater harvesting, greywater reuse and drought-tolerant planting. Material choice considers embodied energy, which is the energy used to extract, make and transport a material, plus durability, local availability, recycled content and toxicity. Life-cycle thinking assesses impacts from cradle to grave, including construction, operation, maintenance and disposal. Suppose a roof of 200 m² receives 800 mm of rain a year and the runoff coefficient (the share of rain that becomes runoff) is 0.8. Harvested water = 200 × 0.8 × 0.8 = 128 m³ a year, about 128,000 litres.

sections.heading: Assessment and adaptation
sections.text: Green building assessment systems score energy, water, materials, indoor environmental quality and site. LEED (United States), BREEAM (United Kingdom) and Green Star (Australia) are examples. National schemes and local standards differ, so check the current official source for the country and project type. Climate adaptation means designing for likely hazards such as heatwaves, floods, drought and sea-level rise. Measures include shading, safe drainage, raised thresholds, permeable surfaces, stored water and passive survivability, which means the building remains usable without power. Adaptation and mitigation are different: mitigation reduces greenhouse gas emissions, while adaptation prepares for effects that are already likely.

keyPoints: Passive design uses orientation, shading, envelope and ventilation to reduce demand before mechanical systems.
Climate zone determines strategy: hot-humid needs shade and cross-ventilation, hot-dry needs thermal mass and night cooling, cold needs insulation and airtightness.
Energy efficiency follows a sequence: reduce demand, use efficient equipment, then add renewable supply.
Life-cycle thinking compares embodied and operational impacts from cradle to grave.
Rainwater yield = roof area × rainfall × runoff coefficient, using consistent units.
Green rating systems and local standards differ by country, so check the current official scheme.

en.title: Heritage Conservation and Adaptive Reuse
en.short: Values-based conservation, documentation, repair and adaptive reuse of existing buildings.

sections.heading: Values and significance
sections.text: Conservation is the careful management of change in places of heritage value. Heritage value, or significance, is the sum of the qualities that make a place important: historical, architectural, social, spiritual, archaeological and economic. Values-based conservation starts by asking who values the place and why, then tests every proposal against those values. Fabric (the physical material) matters, but so do setting, use and community memory. Heritage law and charters differ by country and change over time; treat them as frameworks to check, not universal rules.

sections.heading: Documenting fabric
sections.text: Documentation records what exists before work starts. A measured survey gives plans, sections and elevations; a condition survey maps defects such as cracks, damp and decay; photographs, archives and oral histories record change and use. The record is a baseline for design, approvals and later repair. In a made-up case, a 1950s cooperative store in Ibadan, Nigeria, is surveyed before reuse: traders describe its social value, while the survey finds cracked concrete columns and a sound roof frame.

sections.heading: Repair principles
sections.text: Repair should be minimal and proportionate: keep sound fabric, mend rather than replace, and use materials compatible with the original. New work should be distinguishable on close inspection and, where possible, reversible, so later generations can undo it. Retain patina, the signs of age that carry evidence. Structural strengthening, damp control and fire safety may be needed, but they should respect significance. Avoid so-called improvements that erase the very values that justify conservation.

sections.heading: Adaptive reuse
sections.text: Adaptive reuse gives an existing building a new use while retaining its significant fabric. The new use must fit the structure, services, access and fire strategy, and must not destroy the values identified. In the Ibadan example, the store becomes a community library and workspace: the concrete frame is repaired, the roof kept, and a separate steel mezzanine carries new loads. Planning and heritage approvals are country-specific; check the current local law and any charter adopted there.

keyPoints: Conservation manages change in places of heritage value; it is not simply freezing a building.
Values-based conservation assesses significance through historical, architectural, social, spiritual and economic values.
Documentation, including measured and condition surveys, provides the baseline for design and approvals.
Repair should be minimal, compatible and, where possible, reversible; retain patina and sound fabric.
Adaptive reuse must fit the structure, services, access and fire strategy without destroying significance.
Heritage law and charters vary by country and change; check the current official framework.

en.title: Digital Design: BIM, Parametric Modelling and Collaboration
en.short: Covers BIM workflows, parametric models, clash detection, visualisation and team coordination.

sections.heading: BIM as shared model
sections.text:
Building information modelling (BIM) is a digital representation of a built asset, holding geometry and information such as materials, quantities and fire ratings. Each discipline authors its own model. A federated model combines these separate models for review without merging ownership.

Files are exchanged through a common data environment (CDE), a controlled store for versions and approvals. IFC (Industry Foundation Classes) is an open exchange format from buildingSMART. ISO 19650 is an international standard for managing information using BIM; it is not a design code.

sections.heading: Parametric modelling
sections.text:
Parametric modelling builds geometry from parameters and constraints. A parameter is a named value, such as a room width; a constraint is a rule, such as keeping two walls parallel. Change the value and the model updates. Components called families can carry rules.

Visual programming tools such as Dynamo and Grasshopper link parameters to logic, so a team can test many options quickly. The output is only as reliable as the inputs and assumptions.

sections.heading: Clash detection
sections.text:
Clash detection combines federated models and checks for interference. A hard clash is a physical overlap, such as a beam passing through a duct. A soft clash is a clearance problem, such as a pipe too close to a wall for maintenance. Not every reported clash is an error, so the team reviews and prioritises.

Case: on a made-up clinic in Kano, the architect, structural engineer and services engineer federate their models. A duct crosses a beam; the team moves the duct on screen before construction, avoiding site rework.

sections.heading: Collaboration and visualisation
sections.text:
Collaboration needs clear roles, model ownership, naming rules, version control and issue tracking. A BIM Execution Plan (BEP) records how the team will work and exchange information.

Visualisation uses renders, walkthroughs and virtual reality for design review and client communication. Use the coordination model for decisions, not only attractive images. Standards, codes and professional registration differ by country, so check the current official source.

keyPoints: BIM holds geometry plus information, not just drawings.
A federated model combines discipline models, while a CDE controls versions and approvals.
Parametric models update when parameters or constraints change.
Clash detection finds hard overlaps and soft clearance problems; review results before acting.
Visualisation supports review and communication but does not replace coordination.
Standards and registration differ by country, so check the official source.

en.title: Professional Practice, Ethics and Contracts
en.short: The architect’s appointment, fees, contracts, liability, insurance and professional ethics.

sections.heading: Role and appointment
sections.text: The architect leads the building design and often administers the construction contract. The appointment should be in writing and state the scope of services, work stages, fee and payment schedule, time, copyright in drawings and dispute procedure. Registration differs by country. In Nigeria architects register with ARCON and may join the NIA; COREN regulates engineering. In the UK the statutory regulator is ARB and RIBA is the professional body. In the US state boards license architects and the AIA is a membership body.

sections.heading: Fees and contracts
sections.text:
Fees may be a percentage of construction cost, a lump sum, a time charge or a fixed fee plus expenses. Professional bodies publish recommended scales, but rates differ by country and year, so check the current scale. Standard forms include JCT (UK), FIDIC (international) and AIA (US); the right one depends on project and country. Check what counts as construction cost.

Example: a fee agreed at 5% of final cost. A cost of ₦40,000,000 gives 40,000,000 × 0.05 = ₦2,000,000. If the cost rises to ₦48,000,000, the fee is ₦2,400,000, an increase of ₦400,000.

sections.heading: Liability and insurance
sections.text: The architect owes duties in contract and a duty of care in tort, meaning to people who may foreseeably be harmed by negligent work. Claims can arise from defective design, weak site supervision or wrong advice. Time limits differ by country. Professional indemnity (PI) insurance covers negligence claims; it is not public liability cover. PI is often written on a claims-made basis, so it responds to claims made while the policy runs, and run-off cover protects a practice that closes.

sections.heading: Ethics and conduct
sections.text: Codes of conduct require competence, honesty, confidentiality, disclosure of conflicts of interest and regard for public safety and the environment. An architect administering a contract must certify fairly between client and contractor, not simply favour the payer. Bribery, false qualifications and copying others’ work without credit are breaches. The registration body can discipline registered architects, and a serious breach can cost the licence in some countries.

keyPoints: Registration differs by country: ARCON in Nigeria, ARB in the UK, state boards in the US.
A written appointment should fix scope, stages, fee, time, copyright in drawings and dispute procedure.
Fees can be a percentage of construction cost, a lump sum or a time charge; scales differ by country and year.
Percentage fee = rate × construction cost.
Professional indemnity insurance covers negligence claims and is often claims-made.
Ethics require fair certification, disclosure of conflicts and competence.

en.title: Building codes, regulations and planning approval
en.short: How building codes, planning permission, zoning, fire, access and energy rules are found and applied.

sections.heading: Codes and approvals
sections.text:
Building regulations are legal minimum standards for construction: structure, fire, health, sanitation, accessibility and energy. Planning permission is separate. It is the local authority’s consent to develop land or change its use. A building permit checks that the drawings meet the regulations, and inspections continue on site. Names and stages differ by country and city; confirm the current process before designing.

In Nigeria, the Architects Registration Council of Nigeria (ARCON) registers architects, while planning and building control are handled by state or city authorities. Do not assume another country’s code applies.

sections.heading: Zoning and planning
sections.text: Zoning divides land into zones and states permitted uses, density, height and setbacks. A shop in a residential zone may need a change of use. In a made-up Lagos case, Ngozi wants a two-storey shop on a residential plot. The architect checks the current state planning law and local zoning map. If shops are not permitted, the client may apply for change of use, redesign for a permitted use, or choose another site. Planning consent can be refused on traffic, drainage or neighbourhood grounds, so early checks save money.

sections.heading: Fire, access, energy
sections.text: Fire safety covers escape routes, fire-resistant compartments, alarms, extinguishers and access for fire appliances. Accessibility means barrier-free routes, ramps, wide doors, accessible toilets and signage. Energy requirements may set insulation, glazing, lighting or renewable targets. These rules differ: the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) applies in the United States, while Nigeria and other countries have their own building codes and planning laws. Never copy another country’s clause numbers or limits; obtain the current edition and local amendments.

sections.heading: Finding current rules
sections.text: Start with the authority: national building code, state or city planning law, and local zoning map. Read the current edition and amendments, use the checklist, and ask building control for clarification. Keep approved drawings and inspection records. A code is a floor, not a design recipe: the architect solves the brief.

keyPoints: Building regulations set minimum technical standards; planning permission controls land use and development; a building permit checks compliance.
Zoning states permitted uses and limits, and a change of use may need planning approval.
Fire safety, accessibility and energy rules vary by country and city.
In Nigeria, ARCON registers architects, while planning and building control are state or city matters.
Check zoning and the planning authority before design, and keep approved drawings and inspection records.
Never copy clause numbers or limits from another country’s code; use the current official edition and local amendments.

en.title: Architectural Research and Critical Writing
en.short: Finding sources, case-study method, citation, integrity and building a clear architectural argument.

sections.heading: Sources and evaluation
sections.text:
Primary sources are original materials: drawings, buildings, interviews and archives. Secondary sources interpret them: books and journal articles. Peer-reviewed articles have been checked by other scholars.

Evaluate every source for authority, currency, relevance, bias and method. A manufacturer’s brochure is evidence of a claim, not neutral proof. Use library databases and the reference lists of articles. If you cite a building regulation, name the country and edition, and check the official text.

sections.heading: Case-study method
sections.text:
A case study examines one project, site or process in depth within stated boundaries. Define a question, choose a typical or revealing case, and gather several kinds of evidence: drawings, documents, observation, photographs and interviews. Triangulation means checking one source against another.

Suppose Amara studies a market rebuilding in Enugu, Nigeria. She interviews traders with consent, measures stalls, and compares council drawings with what was built. When sources disagree, she reports the disagreement. She does not name a trader without permission.

sections.heading: Citation and integrity
sections.text:
Citation shows where an idea, quotation, drawing or data set came from. Plagiarism is presenting someone else’s work or words as your own, whether copied, closely paraphrased or unacknowledged. Quote words with a page number; paraphrase in your own words and still cite. Keep full source details as you read.

Reference managers such as Zotero or Mendeley help, but check entries. Academic integrity also means not inventing data, not altering interviews, and acknowledging help. Styles such as Harvard, APA and Chicago differ; follow your department’s guide.

sections.heading: Writing the argument
sections.text:
An architectural argument makes a claim and supports it with evidence and reasoning. A useful pattern is: claim, because of evidence, therefore conclusion. State your position early, define key terms, and answer the strongest counterargument.

A dissertation proposal argues that a study is worth doing and can be done. It states the research question, the gap in existing writing, the method and sources, ethics and feasibility. Keep description separate from analysis: say what you observed, then what it means.

keyPoints: Primary sources are original materials; secondary sources interpret them.
Evaluate sources for authority, currency, relevance, bias and method.
A case study defines boundaries and uses triangulation to check evidence.
Cite all ideas, quotations, drawings and data; plagiarism includes close paraphrase without acknowledgement.
An architectural argument is a claim supported by evidence and reasoning, with counterarguments answered.
A dissertation proposal states the question, gap, method, sources, ethics and feasibility.

en.title: Advanced Architectural Theory and Criticism
en.short: Covers postcolonial, feminist, ecological and digital debates, critical reading and original argument.

sections.heading: Theory as discourse
sections.text: Theory asks what architecture means and does, not only how it stands. Criticism is reasoned judgement about a building, design or text.
