A discourse is a continuing argument shaped by shared assumptions and language. The canon is the list of works a field treats as central; it is always selective. Advanced reading asks what a text assumes, what evidence it uses and who it leaves out. You then compare texts and state your own position.

sections.heading: Postcolonial and feminist critiques
sections.text: Postcolonial criticism examines how colonial power shaped buildings, cities and architectural knowledge, and how that legacy persists. Edward Said’s Orientalism (1978) argued that Western writing often represented 'the East' as opposite and inferior. Feminist criticism asks how design and theory treat gender, care, safety and labour. It challenges the idea of a neutral user. These perspectives meet in questions about who commissions, designs and uses space. A critical argument must name its context: housing in Nigeria is not identical to housing in the UK.

sections.heading: Ecological and digital debates
sections.text: Ecological criticism asks how buildings and cities relate to ecosystems, energy and climate justice. Ian McHarg’s Design with Nature (1969) argued for designing with natural processes. Current debate adds embodied carbon, the carbon emitted in making and transporting materials, and asks who bears environmental harm. Digital perspectives study computation, parametric design and data. Parametric design uses rules and parameters to generate form. Critics ask whether such tools widen access or concentrate power in firms and regions with fast networks.

sections.heading: Building an argument
sections.text: To build an original argument, state a thesis, support it with evidence from texts and buildings, and answer a counterargument. Example: a fictional council in Kano, Nigeria, plans a market. Amina argues that design should start from existing traders’ routes and stalls. She reads a colonial-era market plan, a feminist study of women traders and an ecological report on heat. Her thesis is that participation is a design method, not a meeting added at the end. She tests against costs and safety.

keyPoints: Theory and criticism examine what architecture means and does, not only how it is built.
Postcolonial criticism traces how colonial power and its categories still shape buildings, cities and architectural knowledge.
Feminist criticism asks how design and theory treat gender, care, safety and labour, and it rejects the idea of a neutral user.
Ecological criticism links buildings and cities to ecosystems, energy, embodied carbon and climate justice.
Digital perspectives study computation, parametric design and data, and ask who gains access and who holds power.
An original argument states a thesis, uses evidence from texts and buildings, and answers a counterargument.

en.title: Research Methods for an Architecture Dissertation
en.short: Framing a dissertation question, choosing qualitative, quantitative or mixed methods, ethics, analysis and writing.

sections.heading: Framing the question
sections.text: A dissertation question must be answerable with your time, data and skills. Start from a problem in architectural practice or theory, then narrow it. Not 'housing in Lagos’ but 'how do residents of a Lagos market describe afternoon thermal comfort?' A good question names the setting, people or buildings, and evidence. From it come aims, objectives and a plan: what you will study, how, when and why it matters. A literature review shows the gap and defines key terms.

sections.heading: Methods and design
sections.text: Quantitative research measures variables with numbers, often by survey or measurement, and tests hypotheses. Qualitative research explores meanings and experiences through interviews, observation or documents, and builds themes. Mixed methods combine both, for example a survey of 240 occupants followed by 12 interviews. Research design is the overall plan linking question, methods, sampling and analysis. Sampling means choosing who or what to study; state how and why. Pilot your tools and keep raw data. Example: 168 returns from 240 questionnaires give 168 ÷ 240 = 0.70, a 70% response rate.

sections.heading: Ethics and analysis
sections.text: Ethics approval is normally required before collecting data from people. Explain consent, anonymity, confidentiality, storage and the right to withdraw. Avoid harm and conflicts of interest. Analysis must match the method. Quantitative analysis uses descriptive statistics such as means and percentages, then suitable tests. Qualitative analysis often uses thematic analysis: transcribe, code, compare codes and form themes. Mixed methods need a clear point of integration, such as comparing survey results with interview themes.

sections.heading: Writing and planning
sections.text: Write early and keep a research log. A common structure is introduction, literature review, methodology, findings, discussion, conclusion and references. The methodology chapter justifies choices and states limits. The discussion answers the question and links findings to literature. Use the referencing style your department requires; styles differ by institution and country. A feasible plan has dates for ethics approval, fieldwork, analysis and drafts, with spare time.

keyPoints: Frame a question that names the setting, participants or buildings, and evidence.
Quantitative methods measure variables; qualitative methods interpret meanings; mixed methods combine both.
Research design links question, sampling, data collection and analysis.
Ethics approval, consent, anonymity and safe data storage are normally required before collecting data from people.
Response rate = returned questionnaires ÷ distributed questionnaires; 168 ÷ 240 = 70%.
Write the methodology to justify choices and the discussion to answer the question.

en.title: Computational Design and Digital Fabrication
en.short: Parametric and algorithmic design, scripting, digital modelling, prototyping and file-to-factory fabrication.

sections.heading: Parametric and algorithmic
sections.text: Parametric design describes geometry through parameters and rules. A parameter is a named value, such as a panel width. A rule links parameters, so changing one value updates the whole model. Algorithmic design goes further: an algorithm is a finite sequence of steps that generates or tests geometry. The designer writes the procedure, not every object. For example, a rule may place a window every 3.0 m along a wall, with width depending on orientation. The result is a family of designs, not one fixed drawing.

sections.heading: Scripting and modelling
sections.text: Scripting means writing code to control a digital model. Visual scripting connects nodes in a graph, as in Grasshopper for Rhino; textual scripting uses a language such as Python. A digital model is a three-dimensional representation with geometry and data, such as material or cost. Because the model is generated by rules, it can be checked and reused. Errors in a script propagate to every output, so test with simple cases. Keep the script readable and record parameter values.

sections.heading: Prototyping and fabrication
sections.text: A prototype is an early physical or digital test. Physical prototypes reveal fit, strength and assembly problems. Digital fabrication uses computer-controlled machines: CNC (computer numerical control) milling cuts material away, laser cutting cuts sheet, and 3D printing adds material in layers. The file-to-factory workflow runs from model to export format, then CAM (computer-aided manufacturing) software, then machine code such as G-code. Design must respect machine limits and tolerances. Tolerances are allowed variations in size; they differ by machine, material and workshop, so check the fabricator’s specification.

sections.heading: Worked example and implications
sections.text: A facade has 20 panels. Panel i has width w = 1.0 + 0.02i metres, for i = 0 to 19. Total width = 20×1.0 + 0.02×(0+1+...+19) = 20 + 0.02×190 = 23.8 m. The average width is 23.8 ÷ 20 = 1.19 m. If all panels were 1.19 m, the total would be the same, but one cutting file would suffice. The parametric version needs 20 files. This is a central design implication: variation increases fabrication and assembly complexity. Computational tools also demand clear data, collaboration and fabrication-aware decisions.

keyPoints: Parametric design defines geometry by parameters and rules; changing a parameter updates the model.
Algorithmic design uses a procedure or algorithm to generate or test geometry.
Scripting, visual or textual, automates model generation; errors propagate to all outputs.
Digital fabrication uses CNC, laser cutting and 3D printing; file-to-factory converts a model to machine code.
For an arithmetic panel series, total width = n·a + d·n(n−1)/2, where a is the first term and d the step.
Tolerances and machine limits vary by machine, material and workshop; check the fabricator’s specification.

en.title: Housing and Informal Urbanism: Incremental Growth and Upgrading
en.short: Housing types, incremental construction, informal settlements, upgrading, tenure, services and participatory design.

sections.heading: Housing types and tenure
sections.text: Housing types include detached, semi-detached and terraced houses, courtyard compounds, walk-up flats and high-rise blocks. In rapidly growing cities, many households live in self-built rooms, backyard rentals or shared tenements. Tenure is the legal or customary basis on which land or housing is held: freehold, leasehold, customary right, public rental or informal occupation. Secure tenure encourages investment, but titling alone may not help tenants or those who cannot pay fees.

sections.heading: Incremental construction
sections.text: Incremental construction means building in phases as savings, materials and confidence allow. A core house provides a serviced room or two that the household can extend later. Sites-and-services schemes, used in many countries, allocate plots with basic roads, water and drainage and secure tenure, leaving house construction to owners. The approach can lower entry costs and support local builders. It works best when plans allow safe structural growth, services can be extended, and loans or technical advice are available.

sections.heading: Informal settlements and upgrading
sections.text: An informal settlement usually has insecure tenure and services that were not planned or are inadequate. Residents often build and improve their own homes and run small businesses. In-situ upgrading improves water, sanitation, drainage, roads, lighting and public space where people already live, reducing disruption to livelihoods. Slum clearance and relocation can break social networks and push people to cheaper, riskier land. The Orangi Pilot Project in Karachi, Pakistan, is a well-known case: residents organised lane-level sewers, the project offered low-cost technical support, and public agencies later handled trunk infrastructure.

sections.heading: Participation and design
sections.text: Participatory design involves residents in decisions, not only in consultation after plans are fixed. Methods include community mapping, transect walks, workshops and full-size prototypes. Architects can contribute service cores, safe stairs, ventilation, courtyards and adaptable room layouts, and can help communities negotiate standards. The policy debate is whether public action should provide housing directly, enable self-build through tenure and services, or combine both. No single model fits every city; local rules, land markets and resident priorities differ.

keyPoints: Housing types range from detached houses to courtyard compounds and high-rise flats; informal rental rooms are common in fast-growing cities.
Tenure is the legal or customary basis of holding land or housing; security matters, but titling alone may exclude tenants.
Incremental construction and sites-and-services schemes let households build over time on serviced plots.
Informal settlements are defined by insecure tenure and inadequate services, not by residents’ skills.
In-situ upgrading is often less disruptive than clearance and relocation; the Orangi Pilot Project shows resident-led sanitation with technical support.
Participatory design involves residents in decisions and can produce adaptable, safe and affordable housing.
